claim: No title was given to the work at the time; the modern title is later; Bosch left no letters or diaries; he did not date his paintings
Bosch born Jheronimus van Aken c. 1450 in 's-Hertogenbosch; grandfather Jan van Aken a painter, four of his five sons painters; father Anthonius
Joined the Brotherhood of Our Lady in 1486/7, a devotional confraternity of about 40 influential citizens
Signed several works 'Jheronimus Bosch'; surname from his town; known only from municipal records and the Brotherhood's account books
About 25 paintings confidently attributed to Bosch today
Triptych of oak panels; height 185.8 cm, centre 172.5 cm wide, wings 76.5 cm each (open c. 3.25 m); dated 1490–1500 by the Prado
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html)

claim: Outer panels in grisaille: Third Day of Creation, vegetation but no human or animal life; tiny God with a Bible on his lap; Psalm 33:9 and 148:5 inscriptions 'For he spake, and it was done' / 'For he commanded, and they were created'
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

claim: Left panel: God presenting Eve to Adam; Bosch first painted the Creation of Eve and changed it (Prado)
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html)

claim: Right panel 'musical Hell' with instruments of torture; tavern inside the tree-man; Belting proposed the tree-man's face as a self-portrait
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

claim: Bird-headed monster on a throne/toilet eating corpses and excreting them; pig in a nun's veil trying to get a man to sign legal documents
Centre panel: nude figures, oversized animals and fruit, pool with riders, five broken structures in the water, two owls at the edges staring at the viewer
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html)

claim: Bosch died 9 August 1516; the triptych is first documented in 1517 in Henry III of Nassau's Brussels palace
Antonio de Beatis, secretary to Cardinal Luigi d'Aragona, travelled 1517–18; in the Nassau palace he wrote 'there are some panels on which bizarre things have been painted'
De Beatis on the great bed: 'the Count had it made because he liked to hold frequent banquets and to see his guests get drunk' (Hale tr.)
Possibly commissioned for a wedding (Harbison)
The 'bed' was probably a lit de justice (ceremonial platform); the triptych likely hung in a hall for councils and court hearings, as an exemplum iustitiae (Koldeweij 2023)
Engelbert II of Nassau commissioned it (Prado; Stedelijk Museum Breda); he died 31 May 1504 and named his nephew Henry III his successor
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://stedelijkmuseumbreda.nl/en/see-do/de-lusten-van-engelbrecht/research ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engelbert_II_of_Nassau

claim: Provenance: René de Châlon 1538–44, William I of Orange 1544–67 (Henry's nephew); expropriated in Brussels by the Duke of Alba, 28 May 1568; to Alba's illegitimate son Fernando de Toledo; taken to Spain
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

claim: Philip II bought it at Fernando de Toledo's posthumous sale in 1591; sent to El Escorial 8 July 1593
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

claim: Philip II, 'the most orthodox Catholic of them all', acquired many Bosch paintings
1593 gift record: a painting 'depicting the variety of the world', known as 'Del Madroño' (strawberry tree)
Late-16th-century evidence that some Spaniards thought Bosch's works tainted with heresy; Sigüenza refuted it

Fray José de Sigüenza (1544–1606), librarian and historian (later prior) of El Escorial, History of the Order of St Jerome c. 1605; called it the 'strawberry plant', about the vanity and transient taste of strawberries
Sigüenza: others paint men as they appear outside; Bosch has the courage to paint them as they are inside
At El Escorial for over 340 years before moving to the Prado (1933 per the Prado's provenance; 1939 per Wikipedia)
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garden_of_Earthly_Delights

claim: Wilhelm Fraenger (1947): centre panel a joyful millennial paradise of innocence; Bosch an Adamite; commissioned by the sect's Grand Master
Fraenger's theory gained popularity, many popular books still accept it; scholars have increasingly turned away from it; Bosch a member of the Brotherhood of Our Lady, not an Adamite
Prado: centre panel 'a false Paradise given over to the sin of lust'; sin begins in Eden and is punished in Hell
source: Museo del Prado, The Garden of Earthly Delights Triptych (collection page, copy: https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/f/21472/files/2025/04/The-Garden-of-Earthly-Delights-Triptych-The-Collection-Museo-Nacional-del-Prado.html)

claim: Feb 2014: Amelia Hamrick, 20, Oklahoma Christian University student (music), late at night, transcribed the notes on a sinner's backside to modern notation, recorded and posted it
Media called it the '500-year-old butt song from Hell'

Earlier transcriptions: Lenneberg 1961, Dixon 1981; recorded by Atrium Musicae (Codex Gluteo) 1978; no clef, so pitch can't be known; faux 'Strichnotation' Bosch also used in the Haywain, the Last Judgement and The Singers in the Egg; music book under the lute
Hamrick: 'I think Bosch may have just been slapping notes up there to make it look like music.'
